reference.source: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine / standard rheumatology references
clinicalPearls: An autoinflammatory sterile bone disease, predominantly of children and adolescents, that despite its name is not caused by infection
Presents with insidious bone pain, local swelling, and tenderness, often with a relapsing and remitting course over months to years
Lesions are characteristically multifocal and commonly affect the metaphyses of long bones, the clavicle, pelvis, and vertebrae
The clavicle is a distinctive site of involvement that is unusual for true bacterial osteomyelitis
It is associated with other inflammatory conditions including inflammatory bowel disease, psoriasis, and palmoplantar pustulosis, and is regarded as the paediatric counterpart of SAPHO syndrome
Whole-body MRI is valuable for detecting clinically silent lesions and defining disease extent
Bone biopsy shows sterile inflammation with negative cultures, helping exclude infection and malignancy
First-line therapy is NSAIDs, with bisphosphonates, TNF inhibitors, or other agents for refractory or spinal disease
reference.pathophysiology: CRMO is a chronic nonbacterial osteitis driven by dysregulated innate immunity, with an imbalance between proinflammatory cytokines (such as TNF and IL-1) and anti-inflammatory signalling leading to sterile osteoclast-mediated bone inflammation and remodelling. Cultures are negative and the process is immune-mediated rather than infective, placing it within the autoinflammatory bone disease spectrum.
additionalDifferentials: Malignant bone tumours (Ewing sarcoma, osteosarcoma) and leukaemia/lymphoma
additionalInvestigations: Whole-body MRI to map multifocal and subclinical lesions
Plain radiographs showing lytic and sclerotic changes
Bone biopsy with microbiology and histology to exclude infection and malignancy
Assessment for associated inflammatory bowel or skin disease
redFlags: Imaging or clinical features that cannot be reliably distinguished from bone malignancy or infection without biopsy
Vertebral involvement with risk of collapse and spinal deformity or neurological compromise
Systemic symptoms or rapidly progressive lesions requiring urgent exclusion of malignancy
Failure to respond to expected therapy prompting reassessment of the diagnosis
reference.prognosis: Many children experience a fluctuating course that eventually settles, but a proportion have persistent or relapsing disease into adulthood, and vertebral lesions may cause lasting deformity; overall the outlook is good with appropriate anti-inflammatory treatment.
pitfalls: Treating sterile lesions as bacterial osteomyelitis with prolonged antibiotics
Failing to biopsy an atypical solitary lesion and missing malignancy
Not performing whole-body imaging and underestimating disease extent
Overlooking associated inflammatory bowel or skin disease
